title: Safe vs. Secure: What the Difference Means for Software Buyers
summary: Safe and secure are not synonyms in software. Learn how standards bodies define each word and how to describe and verify protections without overpromising.
body_markdown:
"Safe" and "secure" are used interchangeably in marketing copy, but in cybersecurity they describe different things. **Safe** means protected from harm that happens by accident or by chance. **Secure** means protected from harm that someone causes on purpose. A product can be one without the other, and a buyer who treats the two words as synonyms will ask the wrong questions in a security review. Below we explain how standards bodies draw the line, why the best systems need both, and how a software company can describe its protections accurately without promising that anything is risk-free.

## TL;DR


- **Safe** is about accidental or random harm, such as a failed backup, a bug, or a misconfiguration. **Secure** is about deliberate, hostile acts, such as an attacker exploiting a vulnerability.
- The two are linked: a system that is not secure cannot be considered safe, according to the UK's national protective security authority.
- Accurate security claims name the specific harm a control prevents. They never say a product is "unhackable" or risk-free.
- Buyers should ask for product security evidence, not only company-level compliance badges.
- Security questionnaires are where these distinctions get tested in practice, so your answers should be consistent, sourced, and current.

## What "safe" and "secure" mean in cybersecurity


The cleanest definitions come from bodies that have to apply them to real systems. The UK's National Protective Security Authority (NPSA)[defines safety as relative freedom from threat or harm caused by random, unintentional acts or events, and security as relative freedom from threat or harm caused by deliberate, unwanted, hostile or malicious acts](https://www.npsa.gov.uk/security-best-practices/build-it-secure/security-informed-safety) . The distinction is about intent: was the harm an accident, or did someone cause it deliberately?


The ITU's standardization sector frames it from the system's point of view. In its description,[security is the ability of a system to protect itself against accidental or intentional attacks, while safety is the ability to operate without risk during normal functions and exceptional conditions](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/studygroups/com17/Pages/safe-intro.aspx) .


In plain software terms:


- A **safe** system keeps working correctly and keeps data intact when things go wrong on their own: a disk fails, a deploy breaks, an employee uploads a file to the wrong folder.
- A **secure** system resists people who are trying to make things go wrong: stolen credentials, injection attacks, malicious insiders, phishing.


One caution before going further. Even the authors of official guidance admit the vocabulary is slippery. In the multinational secure-by-design guidance published by CISA and partner agencies in the US, Australia, Canada, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, and New Zealand, the authors[note that the term "safety" has multiple meanings depending on context](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-06/principles_approaches_for_security-by-design-default_508c.pdf) . That is a reason to define your terms in any document a customer will rely on.


## Safe vs. secure side by side


The table below applies those definitions to everyday software scenarios. It is our own summary of the definitions above, not a formal standard.


Safe Secure


Source of harm Accidents, faults, random events Deliberate, hostile, or malicious acts


Typical question Will the system keep working and keep data intact when something breaks? Can an unauthorized party get in, read, change, or misuse data?


Example risk A failed deployment overwrites a document A stolen password exposes customer records


Typical controls Redundant backups, versioning, testing, failover, change management Access control, encryption, authentication, monitoring, vulnerability management


Evidence a buyer might ask for Recovery objectives, backup practices, uptime history Penetration test summaries, access policies, audit reports


A baramundi explainer on the topic makes a similar split for IT and industrial environments:[safety as protection against physical loss or mishandling, security as logical protection against unauthorized access, disclosure, or use](https://www.baramundi.com/en-gb/blog/article/difference-safety-security/) . Different authors draw the boundary in slightly different places, which is why a precise statement of what is protected, and from what, beats a one-word label every time.


## Why a system needs both


Treating safe and secure as separate boxes to tick is the common mistake. The NPSA's position is that[if a system is not secure, it cannot be considered safe](https://www.npsa.gov.uk/security-best-practices/build-it-secure/security-informed-safety) . It adds that safety systems cannot be assumed immune from attack simply because they are air-gapped or custom-built, and that a safety case is incomplete without considering the impact of security.


The reverse also holds. Vint Cerf, writing in *Communications of the ACM* , argues that[even a system immune to external compromise still carries safety risk](https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656590) . His example is phishing: the malicious content arrives over legitimate, secure pathways such as TLS or a VPN. The channel is protected, yet the user is still harmed. His practical conclusion is that safe networking also depends on users being skeptical and thinking critically,[much like defensive driving](https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656590) , rather than relying only on automated controls.


Google's engineering guide to building secure and reliable systems offers a compact illustration. It explains that[reliability risks are primarily nonmalicious, while security risks come from adversaries actively exploiting vulnerabilities](https://google.github.io/building-secure-and-reliable-systems/raw/ch01.html) , and that the right design response can differ. A system might fail safe by opening, as with a fire exit that unlocks during a power cut, while another should fail secure by staying closed, as with a vault door. Neither choice is universally correct. It depends on which harm you are trying to prevent.


### Where the two collide


The door example shows that safe and secure can pull in opposite directions. Aggressive access restrictions can block legitimate users during an emergency. Generous recovery options can open a path for an attacker. Good design makes the trade-off explicit and documents it, which is exactly what a thorough security reviewer wants to see.


## Can you say "safe and secure"?


Yes, and the pairing is not redundant when each word carries its own meaning. "Safe and secure" is accurate when you can say what you do about accidental harm (backups, versioning, testing, recovery) and what you do about deliberate harm (access control, encryption, monitoring). It becomes empty when it is a slogan with nothing behind it.


A useful test for any sentence on a product page: could a reader ask "safe from what?" and get an answer in the next sentence? If not, rewrite it. "Your data is safe with us" says nothing. "Documents are versioned, so an accidental overwrite can be reversed, and access is limited by role" says two specific things.


## How to describe your protections accurately


Software companies feel pressure to sound bulletproof. Regulators and security guidance push the other way, toward reasonable, documented, proportionate claims. Here is how to write them.


### 1. Name the harm and the control


Pair every claim with the threat it addresses. The FTC's business guide, *Start with Security* , tells companies to[assess their options and make reasonable choices based on their business and the sensitivity of the information](https://search.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/920a_start_with_security_en_aug2023_508_final_0.pdf) , and to protect information throughout its lifecycle, not just while it is in transit. Your public language should mirror that logic: sensitivity of data, choice of control, lifecycle coverage.


### 2. Separate company security from product security


CISA draws a distinction that buyers and vendors both need.[Enterprise security protects a company's own infrastructure, while product security covers what a manufacturer does to make the delivered software secure against attackers](https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2024/240806.pdf) . A vendor's SOC 2 report or ISO certificate speaks mainly to the first. Be clear which one a given claim supports.


### 3. Treat security as a property of use, not a feature


Systems engineers point out that safety and security are[dynamic properties of how a system is used, not static features](https://systems.chrysaetos.org/chapter-46.html) , and that a mechanism like encryption is only one piece of a solution. So avoid language like "protected by encryption" as if that closes the question. Say what is encrypted, where, and what other controls surround it.


### 4. Anchor to a framework


Frameworks give claims a shared vocabulary. NIST's Special Publication 800-37 Revision 2 describes a[Risk Management Framework that incorporates security and privacy throughout the system development life cycle](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-37r2.pdf) . Referencing a recognized framework tells reviewers how you manage risk, rather than asking them to take a promise on faith.


### 5. Never promise zero risk


No credible guidance says a product can be risk-free. Write "designed to reduce the risk of unauthorized access" rather than "cannot be breached." Precise, bounded statements age better, survive legal review, and read as more trustworthy to experienced buyers.


## What buyers should demand


If you are on the buying side, CISA's guidance is direct: customers should[explicitly demand product security, not just general enterprise compliance, during procurement](https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2024/240806.pdf) . The agency's broader secure-by-design push asks manufacturers to[stop leaving customers to do constant damage control](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-06/principles_approaches_for_security-by-design-default_508c.pdf) and to treat security as a core business goal.


In practice, a vendor review should cover both halves of the vocabulary:


1. **Safety evidence:** backup and recovery practices, change management, versioning, and incident history for non-malicious failures.
2. **Security evidence:** access control model, authentication options, encryption approach, vulnerability handling, and independent assessments.
3. **Scope:** which of those apply to the product you are buying, not just the vendor's corporate network.
4. **Consistency:** whether answers match across the security questionnaire, the trust page, and the contract.

## Where questionnaires expose the gap


Security questionnaires are where vague "safe and secure" language gets tested. A prospect sends 200 questions about encryption, access reviews, backup testing, and incident response. Answers drafted by different people, from stale documents, will contradict one another, and an inconsistent answer about backups (a safety control) or access (a security control) is exactly what slows a deal.


The fix is a single, current source of truth. When answers come from a maintained knowledge base with document versioning, each response says the same thing about what is protected and how. ## A short checklist for your next claim


Before you publish or send any statement about protection, run it through these questions:


- Does it say what is protected and from what: accident, attacker, or both?
- Is the control named, rather than implied by a word like "safe"?
- Does it apply to the product, or only to your company's internal environment?
- Is it consistent with your trust page, policies, and previous questionnaire answers?
- Does it avoid promising zero risk?
- Is there an owner and a review date, so it does not go stale?


Teams that keep this discipline find that reviews move faster, because reviewers spend less time probing vague language. ## FAQ


### What is the difference between safe and secure?


Safe refers to protection from accidental or random harm, while secure refers to protection from deliberate, hostile acts. The UK's NPSA uses exactly this split, defining[safety around unintentional events and security around malicious ones](https://www.npsa.gov.uk/security-best-practices/build-it-secure/security-informed-safety) . Most real systems need both.


### Can a system be secure but not safe?


Yes. A system can resist attackers and still harm users or lose data through errors, misconfiguration, or deceptive content. Vint Cerf's phishing example shows how[secure channels can still carry hazardous content](https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656590) . That is why user awareness and recovery planning sit alongside technical controls.


### Is it redundant to say "safe and secure"?


Not when each word carries a specific meaning. Use it when you can explain what you do about accidents (backups, versioning, testing) and about attacks (access control, encryption, monitoring). If you cannot, drop the phrase and describe the controls instead.


### How should a software company describe its security without overpromising?


Name the threat and the control, state whether the claim covers the product or the company, and avoid absolute words such as "unhackable." The FTC advises companies to[make reasonable choices based on their business and the sensitivity of the information](https://search.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/920a_start_with_security_en_aug2023_508_final_0.pdf) they hold. Reference a recognized framework where it applies.


### What should buyers ask vendors about security?


Ask about product security specifically, not only corporate certifications, as CISA recommends in its[guide for software customers](https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2024/240806.pdf) . Cover access control, encryption, backup and recovery, vulnerability handling, and independent assessments. Then check that written answers match across every document the vendor provides.
